title: Wasserman's Inc. v. Township of Middletown
lead: A township cancelled a long-term store lease, triggering a negotiated revenue-based payment whose relationship to actual loss remained uncertain.
proceedings: Law Division enforced the lease and awarded cancellation payments with interest.
New Jersey Supreme Court upheld the lease and improvement award but remanded the gross-receipts provision.
limits: The gross-receipts provision was neither finally enforced nor finally invalidated. The source reports a one-cent discrepancy between its total and components. Consumer contracts and later bidding requirements were not the governing issues.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: A long lease secures the store’s location
paragraphs: Wasserman’s operated a general store on Middletown Township land from 1948 to 1968. The parcel contained about 20,500 square feet and a 3,200-square-foot store. The Township advertised a new lease in 1969, rejected Wasserman’s sole bid, and advertised again in May 1970. Again the only bidder, Wasserman’s negotiated a lease approved that September and signed May 21, 1971. The Township valued the property at $47,500. The thirty-year term carried fixed monthly rent of $458.33 without escalation.

The bid specifications contemplated proportional reimbursement for improvements upon cancellation. The signed contract also required 25% of average annual gross receipts over the preceding three complete fiscal years, a term absent from the solicitation. Improvement reimbursement depended on the unexpired portion of the term.

Wasserman’s spent $142,336.01 in 1971 to renovate and expand the store to about 5,600 square feet. In 1973 it sold the business and sublet to Rocco Laurino doing business as Jo-Ro, Inc., for $1,850 monthly, agreeing how to allocate cancellation proceeds. Later buyers purchased Jo-Ro’s stock for $95,000 on a representation that the lease continued. The Township allowed the subletting.

sections.title: The Township cancels and sells the land
sections.cue: The occupants enforce the payment clauses
paragraphs: In December 1987 the Township gave notice cancelling the lease effective December 31, 1988. The occupants vacated without another business location. In June 1989 the Township auctioned the land for $610,000.

Plaintiffs sued for the cancellation payments. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the Law Division upheld the lease and provision, later entering a reported $346,058.44 judgment plus 10% prejudgment interest. Its stated components were $55,748.27 for improvements and $290,310.18 based on receipts; those components exceed the reported total by one cent. The Appellate Division affirmed. The Township initially contested both payments but conceded the improvement obligation in the Supreme Court.
It continued to argue that officials lacked authority to add the gross-receipts provision and that changing the solicitation violated public-contract requirements.

sections.title: The lease was lawfully made
sections.cue: Its agreed remedy still requires scrutiny
paragraphs: Justice Pollock’s unanimous New Jersey Supreme Court opinion applied the statute in force when the parties signed, New Jersey Statutes Annotated section 40:60-42,, which did not require bidding for this private lease. Voluntary advertising did not import an inapplicable bidding regime. Wasserman’s had been the only bidder twice; the record established neither bad faith, corruption, municipal detriment, nor that the added term would have attracted another bidder. It instead supported negotiated concessions needed to secure the lease.

A replacement bidding statute took effect six weeks after signing. Neither text nor history supported retroactivity. Belated invalidation also risked contract-clause concerns, although the court did not decide a constitutional violation.

The court nevertheless tested the revenue-based payment for reasonableness as compensation rather than punishment. Difficulty estimating damages informed that inquiry instead of operating as a mechanically separate requirement. Actual loss could illuminate the reasonableness of anticipated harm; labels and subjective characterizations did not control. Commercial stipulations between parties of comparable bargaining power were presumptively reasonable, with production and persuasion burdens on the challenger. Consumer contracts were reserved, and unfairness or unconscionability could still matter.

sections.title: Gross receipts do not establish cancellation loss
paragraphs: Gross receipts omit operating costs and expenses specifically attributable to termination. A revenue formula could reimburse saved expenses or create a windfall, but no rule made every percentage of receipts invalid. Here Jo-Ro reported $3,483,722.25 in receipts for 1985–1987, or $1,161,240.75 annually, producing the claimed $290,310.18. Tax returns showed profits of only $3,649 and $414, followed by a $323 loss. Tax and economic losses differ, but those figures raised a serious question if they reflected actual performance.

The Law Division needed to examine using receipts regardless of cancellation date, choosing one-quarter of a year’s average instead of the remaining term, the parties’ reasons, mitigation, market rents, replacement space, and relocation or other termination losses. Enforceability was legal, but necessary underlying facts were missing. The Township retained the burden of proving unreasonableness.

The Supreme Court affirmed the lease’s validity and the $55,748.27 improvement award, reversed in part, and remanded for the necessary damages proceedings. It did not finally uphold or invalidate the separate gross-receipts payment.
